# Discussion and recommendations 
Lower scores on the metrics associated with the analytical protocol indicate that descriptions were incomplete or that necessary details were glossed over. As these are also the more technical aspects of data-led publications, this may very well be due to word count restraints, the desire by authors not to repeat themselves across multiple publications if settings or protocols are identical to previous work (as indicated in some publications were citations are given to previous work in the methodology section), an assumption by specialists that this information is self-explanatory or irrelevant to the reader, or a combination of these factors. 

Stages related to computational reproducibility that scored low indicated a range of experiences: from missing information that made reproduction impossible (such as how zero/bdl values were handled to missing parameters on multi-variate statistics) to reproduction with a certain level of friction (information was present but needed to be pulled from different tables/appendices or data were provided in formats that were error-prone for re-use). Notably, stage 2 (inclusion of original data) scored relatively low with an average of 1.2 (@fig-bar-plot), due to the inclusion of re-use friction as a contributing factor in our scoring system and the relatively common use of tables in text or digital supplements of PDF or Microsoft Word files. For stages 10 and 11, it should be borne in mind that of the 100 articles that were analysed, 79 did not include any statistical analyses (scoring an NA). Similarly, 21 articles did not include any visualisations of compositional data (stage 12). This means the overall scores on these stages are based on only a subsection of the dataset.

About half of the surveyed articles in each stage were already fully reproducible (score 2), and, except for stage 5, only a small number of articles per stage was not reproducible (score 0). This shows that the community is already well aware of the topic while room for improvement remains. The reproducibility index presented here already provides pointers for authors, reviewers, and editors for further increasing the reproducibility of research output. For the topics with the highest potential for improvement, additional recommendations will be provided below: analytical protocols, handling of analytical uncertainty, transparency in data treatment, adoption of standardised terminologies, and visualisation. 

## Recording analytical protocols and decision trajectories
To improve the reproducibility of analytical methods and at the same time achieve higher transparency of methodological choices to better inform data re-use, many methodology sections need to be more elaborate. Based on the literature survey, this especially concerns information about how and where objects where sampled, the classification of data as outliers and their handling, normalisation of data and data transformation in e.g. preparation for statistical analysis. Given the preponderance of digital publishing formats, the use of accompanying open access data publications with permissible licenses should be encouraged by (co-)authors, reviewers and editors. This recommendation mirrors many journal guidelines. The advantages of such data publications are clear: They allow the space to provide full details without taking away from the overall flow of an article’s arguments and impacting the word limit for an article. This may be especially useful for studies employing multiple analytical techniques and to outline sampling decisions and/or deviations from standard analytical protocols. Further, they allow that methodological information and data are accessible by everyone even if the article is not published in open access. 
Some surveyed publications kept their methodology sections brief by citing analytical protocols (usually their own), which is an effective alternate strategy. However, it puts more of the onus of chasing down references on the re-user and can restrict access to this information if the re-user does not have access to the cited publication. Especially with regards to the latter, we encourage authors to consider alternative options to make their analytical protocols citable, such as the free and open access platform [protocols.io](https://www.protocols.io/). 

## Analytical uncertainty
Stage 5, the inclusion of analytical uncertainties in the reported data, was the most non-reproducible stage among the surveyed literature with almost a fifth of the surveyed articles receiving a score of 0. Most often, analytical uncertainties were not provided for compositional data, especially data obtained by XRF and SEM methods. Consequently, also many plots of compositional data do not include the analytical uncertainties as error bars and may result in a misleading representation of the data. Like all measured quantities, compositional data are not a precise value but probability distributions, with the mean as the most likely value and a value describing the probability distribution’s spread, usually the standard variation. This means that reporting only the mean but not the analytical uncertainty can create a wrong impression of the data and could, e.g., result in the erroneous assignments of artefacts to compositional groups. Moreover, extracting the analytical uncertainties of measurement data from the instrument software is usually straightforward; for example, they are included in the standard output of pXRF instruments. Therefore, researchers must always include analytical uncertainties for all measured values in their research output, and reviewers and editors should always request this information from the authors. 

## Computational reproducibility and transparency 
While the analytical protocols encountered in the bibliographic analysis were incredibly varied, the data analytics (statistical tests and forms of visualisation) were fairly standardised across the spectrum. This uniformity of computational approaches makes this part of the research process uniquely suited to the type of computational and formal reproducibility efforts as espoused by @Marwick2025. However, a detailed recording of computational analytics in coded scripts may be beyond the skill sets of many researchers and, while transparency is to be encouraged, a reasonable trade-off is sometimes made for lack of incentives or time pressure [@abdill_how-guide_2024]. The latter may be especially pressing for small-scale studies, studies with a single author, studies by early career researchers, or studies without large amounts of funding backing them. Furthermore, if every study going forward were to produce their own hard-coded data pipeline, this would create a great wealth of methodologies and approaches, which does not necessarily lead to further standardisation of approaches or adoption of methodologies by other scholars. 

Assumptions about how analytical data are constructed or are expected to behave must be made explicit and inform the choice for an appropriate statistical test or necessary data transformation. An example might be the use of kernel density estimates in cases where a normal or Gaussian distribution cannot be assumed [@baxter_testing_1998; @hsu_application_2018].  

## Adoption of standardised terminologies
Reproducibility of research greatly benefits from avoiding ambiguity in the terms and abbreviations used and, especially if ambiguity cannot be avoided, referring to established definitions for them. Thesauri such as the Arts and Architecture Thesaurus of the Getty Research Institute [@harpring_development_2010] are predestined for this task, and so are controlled vocabularies if they include definitions of the terms. Adopting their use and actively referring to terms in them lower barriers for readers unfamiliar with regional specifics by making it easy to find definitions. In addition, it facilitates comparison between publications and the combination of datasets. While use of standard terminologies may not directly contribute to reproducibility in the sense of analytical or computational reproducibility, they contribute to the replicability of research. 

## Visualisation
Visualisations in a little over one third of the articles could not or only partially reproduced. Reasons can be generally grouped into three cases: the plot itself, hampered connections between the reported and the visualised data and a detachment of reported data and visualisation. Reproducibility barriers created by the visualisation itself are rare and represent, for example, regressions lines or ellipses without any further explanation. Consequently, their meaning cannot be understood: is, for example, an ellipsis a statistical confidence ellipsis or is it an annotation to highlight specific parts of the data? 
More abundant were hampered links between the reported data and the visualised data. These cases include differences between reported and visualised values for individual data points, probably indicating typos or transposed digits. They also include cases with insufficient contextual information, meaning that the dataset was plotted correctly but e.g. the variable used for grouping (e.g. by point colour) could not be found in the data or that data were selected and/or grouped according to imprecisely defined criteria, such as the absence of the threshold applied to differentiate between regular and high-tin bronzes. Finally, a few articles reported only averages of individual measurements while plotting the individual readings. 
Most often, however, plots are not reproducible as a direct consequence of non-reproducible data transformation and processing, leading to a detachment of the visualisation from the reported data. A particularly abundant case is the undocumented handling of values below the detection limit or the absence of data points, presumably outliers. Similarly, most visualisations of multi-variate statistics outcomes such as dendrograms could be reproduced because the statistics itself was not reproducible. 
All these findings highlight the importance of data pipelines for data processing, including visualisation, and the publication of raw data alongside it in the article or accompanying data publication: This combination guarantees that the link between the data and the visualisations cannot be break. Because every step is recorded, the risk for human error is significantly reduced. In fact, any direct human interaction with the dataset can be eliminated if the pipeline starts directly at the raw data. Moreover, reviewers and other persons can run the pipeline as well, providing an easy way to verify that data processing is reproducible. 

## Data availability statements
We already highlighted in the introduction the opportunity within this study to analyse compliance with data availability statement requirements (see criticism in @Marwick2025). Some patterns are observable in how these statements are used, some of which seem to indicate a misunderstanding of what they mean and some seem specific to certain journal policies. 
13 publications did not feature a data availability statement, mostly in journals that do not usually feature them (METALLA) or only recently introduced them (Historical Metallurgy). It is also worth noting that two articles were found without such statements in the Journal of Archaeological Science, which employs a reproducibility editor. 

Just over a third of all surveyed articles (37) featured data availability statements that accurately and completely summarised the availability of data in the publication: when data were included in the manuscript, the supplement or both, this was correctly noted. That makes the current state of use for data availability statements seem rather dire, but it is a little more complicated than that. 

Of the remaining 50 articles, five contained data in a different format than the availability statement claimed. 13 of them claimed data would be made available upon request but still provided it in tables or supplements. Maybe this suggests that less processed data or data in a different format could be accessed. Finally, 32 publications included a statement claiming no datasets were generated or analysed, even though this was demonstrably the case and data were included in tables or supplements. This particular situation was mostly found in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, suggesting that this may be a default option in the submission portal. 

Based on these situation, the usefulness of data availability statements could be questioned. However, they undeniably provide a quick orientation where data can be found or why it is not provided. Therefore, these findings should be interpret as encouragement for editors and reviewers to become more rigorous in the application of the editorial policies, and a call to all authors to be more attentive when writing data availability statements. 

## A way forward: ASTR
A promising way forward towards increased computational reproducibility of analytical data is the adoption of the community-driven reporting format recently suggested by the developers of the R package ASTR “Archaeometric Standards and Tools in R”. In contrast to previous suggestions [e.g., @staudigel_electronic_2003; @case_gnd_guide_2024], this community-driven reporting format defines a set of conventions that reduces implicit information in datasets to a minimum and makes them easy to read for machines and humans alike. It is software and language agnostic and compliant datasets can be prepared with any spreadsheet software. The accompanying R package [@astr] increases transparency and reproducibility of data pipelines by providing a citable and open source toolbox for common steps in the discipline’s data pipeline, such as data import, data transformation, visualisation, and statistics. While many of the functions in the ASTR package do not depend on a dataset in the reporting format, adhering to it provides a lot of convenience such as automatic conversion of units and dedicated functions for data subsetting. 

<!-- update ASTR citation -->

# Conclusions
The inherently destructive nature of archaeological research makes reproducibility a key criteria for data quality in the discipline, and the archaeological sciences are no different, especially if invasive and destructive sampling and analytical methods are involved. To investigate how reproducible the archaeological sciences currently are, a bibliographic survey was carried out on research articles publishing compositional or isotopic data on an archaeometallurgical topic in the field’s major journals between November 2025 and January 2026. A quantifiable description of an article’s reproducibility was gained through an index of 13 stages, each with a possible score of 0, 1 or 2, representing no, partial or full reproducibility. In contrast to previous studies, the stages were defined from a practitioner’s perspective and therefore combine for the first time aspects of analytical and computational reproducibility. 

The bibliographic survey shows an overall good reproducibility with about 50% of the articles in each stage being fully reproducible, a median score of 16 per article and a maximum score of 25 out of 26. However, notable differences between stages can be observed. Potential for improving reproducibility was identified in five major areas: analytical protocols, handling of analytical uncertainty, transparency in data treatment, adoption of standardised terminologies, and visualisation. Recommendations for how reproducibility can be improved are given for each of the topics. Most importantly, data publications provide the option to record the necessary details about the sampling and analytical protocols that can often not be included in the main article due to length restrictions. The adoption of data pipelines for data processing and transformation, ideally starting from the raw data, ensures full reproducibility of data processing and transformation, including statistical tests and visualisations. 

While the surveyed literature is restricted to archaeometallurgical articles, similar findings are expected when all fields in the archaeological sciences creating and publishing compositional and isotopic data would be included. The recommendations can be readily adopted by them. More formalised insights into the state of reproducibility for other fields data types are nevertheless required, and the presented index can serve as the starting points for this endeavour. These insights can be used to develop best practices and tools tailored for the archaeological sciences, such as the best practices for pXRF data [@johnson_best_2024], serving as common reference points. Ideally, such best practices are developed in collaboration with neighbouring fields that use the same analytical methods: Because of the huge variety of methods and data types, the archaeological sciences are in the unique position to spearhead and harmonise such efforts.
